SEXUAL HEALTH / GUM__HIV Testing (4th-ge:
HIV testing uses a 4th-generation antigen/antibody combination immunoassay to diagnose infection, alongside CD4 count to gauge immune status and HIV viral load to monitor response to antiretroviral therapy (ART). Together these answer three separate questions: Is the person infected?, How damaged is their immune system? and Is treatment working?

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Testing is offered for diagnosis (symptoms, seroconversion illness, risk exposure), as universal opt-out screening in high-prevalence areas, GUM/sexual-health clinics and antenatal care, and for monitoring established infection. The 4th-generation assay is a combined test that detects both p24 antigen and anti-HIV antibodies. Because p24 antigen appears before antibodies, this shortens the window period to about 4 weeks.

🧪4th-gen Ag/Ab assay
Detects p24 antigen + antibody; screening test for diagnosis
🛡️CD4 count
Marker of immune status & opportunistic-infection risk
📉Viral load
HIV RNA copies/mL; measures response to ART
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A venous blood sample is sent for the laboratory 4th-generation assay; point-of-care fingerprick tests also exist but a reactive result always needs laboratory confirmation. Consent is required but testing is opt-out in many settings (the patient is told a test will be done unless they decline). Timing relative to exposure is critical:

A test taken too soon may miss very recent infection - the result must be interpreted against the date of the last risk exposure.
A reactive screening result is followed by a second, supplementary confirmatory assay on the same or a fresh sample before any diagnosis is given.
Once diagnosed, CD4 count and baseline viral load are measured to stage disease and guide treatment, then viral load is repeated to confirm suppression on ART.
3INTERPRETATION
4th-gen lab test negative at ≥45 days (about 6–7 weeks) after exposure→Reliably excludes HIV - no further testing needed for that exposure
Reactive screening assay→Confirm with a supplementary/confirmatory assay before making the diagnosis
Confirmed HIV (positive after the confirmatory assay)→refer to specialist HIV care and start antiretroviral therapy (ART) promptly, regardless of CD4 (aiming for an undetectable viral load); add opportunistic-infection prophylaxis if CD4 <200. HIV ›
CD4 <200 cells/mm³→AIDS-defining threshold; high opportunistic-infection risk - start prophylaxis (e.g. co-trimoxazole for PCP)
Viral load undetectable on ART→Effective treatment; Undetectable = Untransmittable (U=U)
4PITFALLS, PEP & SAFETY

The main pitfall is the window period: an early negative result does not exclude very recent infection, so a 4th-generation test should be repeated at 45 days (about 6–7 weeks) after the last exposure. After a significant exposure, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP / PEPSE) should be started as soon as possible and within 72 hours. A seroconversion illness (fever, rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy) can occur before antibodies are detectable - if suspected, the p24 antigen component or a viral load may be positive even when antibody is not yet formed.

🚩 The WINDOW PERIOD means an early negative test does NOT exclude very recent infection - repeat a 4th-gen assay at 45 days after exposure. Offer PEP within 72 hours of a high-risk exposure and never delay while waiting for results. Suspect acute HIV in anyone with a seroconversion illness (fever, rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy), as antibodies may not yet be detectable.
🎓 4th-gen Ag/Ab assay detects p24 antigen + antibody, window ~4 weeks (retest at 45 days). CD4 <200 defines AIDS-level risk. Undetectable viral load = untransmittable (U=U). PEP within 72h.
SEXUAL HEALTH / GUM__STI NAAT — Multi-si:
A nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) is the first-line, most sensitive test for the common bacterial sexually transmitted infections. It amplifies pathogen DNA/RNA to confirm Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Mycoplasma genitalium — but it only diagnoses infection at the sites you actually sample, so the specimen strategy is driven entirely by the sexual history.

1Indication & principle

NAAT is the first-line diagnostic for chlamydia and gonorrhoea and the test of choice for M. genitalium in persistent non-gonococcal urethritis/cervicitis. It amplifies target nucleic acid, giving far greater sensitivity than culture, and works on non-invasive samples (urine, self-taken swabs).

🧫C. trachomatis
Commonest bacterial STI; often asymptomatic
🦠N. gonorrhoeae
NAAT screens; culture needed for sensitivities
🧪M. genitalium
Persistent NGU/cervicitis; macrolide resistance common
2How it is performed — specimen by site
Women: self-taken vulvovaginal swab is the most sensitive genital specimen (preferred over urine).
Men: first-void urine (first part of the stream, ideally ≥1 hour since last passing urine).
Extragenital: add pharyngeal and rectal swabs where there has been oral or anal exposure.
3Interpretation & onward action
Asymptomatic screening (under-25s / opportunistic)→NAAT on first-void urine (men) or self-taken vulvovaginal swab (women)
MSM or any oral/anal sexual exposure→Add pharyngeal + rectal NAAT — genital-only testing misses extragenital infection
Gonorrhoea NAAT positive→Take a culture BEFORE treatment to test antibiotic sensitivities, then treat with IM ceftriaxone
Persistent non-gonococcal urethritis / cervicitis→Test for M. genitalium and its macrolide-resistance markers
Chlamydia NAAT positive→doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days (first-line; azithromycin if contraindicated/pregnancy) and arrange partner notification. Chlamydia ›
4Pitfalls & limitations
NAAT detects nucleic acid, not viable organisms — it gives no antibiotic-sensitivity data, so gonorrhoea still needs culture.
A negative genital NAAT does not exclude throat or rectal infection if those sites were not sampled.
Blind azithromycin for M. genitalium risks driving macrolide resistance — check resistance markers first.
🚩 A genital-only NAAT MISSES pharyngeal and rectal infection — take throat and rectal swabs according to the sexual history or infections go undiagnosed and transmission continues. Every positive gonorrhoea NAAT must be backed by culture for sensitivities because of rising antimicrobial resistance, and M. genitalium must NOT be treated blindly with azithromycin owing to widespread macrolide resistance.
🎓 NAAT is first-line and most sensitive. In women the vulvovaginal swab beats urine; ALWAYS add pharyngeal and rectal swabs if there has been oral or anal exposure; and ALWAYS culture gonorrhoea for sensitivities before treating.
SEXUAL HEALTH / GUM__Gonorrhoea Culture:
Gonorrhoea culture & sensitivities is a bacteriological test in which a charcoal (Amies) transport swab is taken from an infected site and plated on selective media to grow Neisseria gonorrhoeae and, critically, to obtain its antibiotic sensitivities. In an era of escalating gonococcal resistance it is the only way to confirm which antimicrobial will actually work, so a culture must be taken BEFORE any antibiotic is given.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Culture is indicated whenever gonorrhoea is suspected clinically or a NAAT is positive. NAAT is exquisitely sensitive for detecting gonococcal DNA but it CANNOT provide antibiotic sensitivities — it only tells you the organism is present, not what will kill it. Because N. gonorrhoeae is developing resistance across multiple antibiotic classes, a live culture is essential to guide and audit therapy.

Take culture before starting antibiotics, otherwise the organism will not grow.
N. gonorrhoeae is a fastidious, fragile Gram-negative diplococcus that dies quickly outside the body.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

A charcoal swab (Amies transport medium, usually black-topped) is used to sample the relevant site: urethra, endocervix, rectum, pharynx or eye, depending on exposure. The charcoal neutralises toxic fatty acids and metabolites and keeps the delicate organism viable during transport. The swab is plated onto selective media (e.g. modified Thayer-Martin/GC agar) and incubated in a CO₂-enriched atmosphere. The sample must reach the laboratory promptly.

🧪Charcoal swab
Amies transport medium; preserves the fragile gonococcus for culture
📍Sites
Urethra, endocervix, rectum, pharynx or eye
🔬Microscopy
Gram-negative intracellular diplococci on urethral smear
🧫Selective media
GC/Thayer-Martin agar in CO₂; yields the isolate for sensitivities
3INTERPRETATION
Gonorrhoea NAAT positive→Take a culture on a charcoal swab BEFORE giving antibiotics to allow sensitivity testing
Gram-negative intracellular diplococci on urethral smear→Presumptive gonorrhoea; culture confirms and provides sensitivities
Sample must reach the lab promptly→The organism is delicate and dies on delay, giving a false-negative culture
Culture grows N. gonorrhoeae with sensitivities→First-line treatment is ceftriaxone single IM dose, tailored to the sensitivity result
4PITFALLS & SAFETY
A dry, delayed or non-charcoal swab lets the organism die, producing a false-negative culture despite active infection.
NAAT alone is not enough — it confirms infection but gives no sensitivities, so culture is still needed.
Arrange a test of cure after treatment to confirm eradication, given resistance risk.
🚩 Neisseria gonorrhoeae has escalating antimicrobial resistance, including to cephalosporins. ALWAYS take a culture with sensitivities before treatment and arrange a test of cure — NAAT alone cannot provide antibiotic sensitivities. Watch for serious complications: disseminated gonococcal infection (arthritis, tenosynovitis, pustular rash) and gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum.
🎓 The charcoal swab preserves the fragile gonococcus for CULTURE — always culture before treating to guide therapy against a resistant organism. First-line is IM ceftriaxone with a test of cure.
SEXUAL HEALTH / GUM__Urethral Smear & Gr:
The urethral smear with Gram stain is a rapid, near-patient microscopy test performed in a genitourinary medicine (GUM) clinic on a symptomatic patient. A specimen from the urethra (or cervix/vagina) is smeared, Gram-stained and examined under oil-immersion. It gives an immediate presumptive diagnosis of urethritis and, if Gram-negative intracellular diplococci are seen, of gonorrhoea — allowing treatment to begin at the same visit while nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) and culture are still pending.

1Indication & principle

Used in symptomatic patients — typically a man with urethral discharge or dysuria — to confirm urethritis and split it into gonococcal versus non-gonococcal at the bedside.

Polymorphonuclear leucocytes (PMNs) on the smear are the objective marker of urethral inflammation (urethritis).
Gram-negative intracellular diplococci — kidney-bean-shaped organisms inside PMNs — represent Neisseria gonorrhoeae and distinguish gonococcal from non-gonococcal urethritis.
2How it is performed

Ideally the patient has not passed urine for ≥2 hours (to avoid washing out discharge and PMNs).

A plastic loop or swab collects a sample of discharge / material from ~1–2 cm inside the anterior urethra.
The material is rolled onto a glass slide, air-dried, heat-fixed and Gram-stained (crystal violet → iodine → decolouriser → safranin counterstain).
The slide is read under oil-immersion (×1000) high-power fields; PMNs are counted and organisms sought within them.
3Interpretation & cut-offs
≥5 PMNs per high-power field (urethral smear) WITH Gram-negative intracellular diplococci→Gonococcal urethritis — treat for gonorrhoea; confirm with culture (for sensitivities) and NAAT
PMNs present but NO diplococci seen→Non-gonococcal urethritis — treat empirically for chlamydia / M. genitalium (e.g. doxycycline)
Clue cells on wet/Gram film (epithelial cells studded with bacteria)→Bacterial vaginosis
No PMNs and asymptomatic→Low likelihood of urethritis (but does not exclude infection)
🧫PMNs
Marker of urethritis; ≥5 per HPF on urethral smear
🧪GNID
Gram-negative intracellular diplococci = gonorrhoea
💊NGU
PMNs, no diplococci → treat for chlamydia
🔬Clue cells
Epithelial cells coated in bacteria → BV
4Pitfalls & limitations
Microscopy is highly operator-dependent and needs a symptomatic patient with adequate discharge.
Sensitivity for gonorrhoea is good (>90%) in symptomatic men but poor in women and at pharyngeal / rectal sites, where NAAT is required.
Recent voiding, antibiotics or asymptomatic infection can all give a falsely negative smear.
🚩 Microscopy is INSENSITIVE in asymptomatic patients and in female, pharyngeal and rectal infection — a negative smear does NOT exclude gonorrhoea or chlamydia. Always send a NAAT (and culture for gonorrhoea before treating, to guide antimicrobial sensitivities), treat non-gonococcal urethritis empirically for chlamydia, and offer partner notification.
🎓 Urethral smear shorthand: PMNs = urethritis; Gram-negative intracellular diplococci = gonorrhoea; PMNs without diplococci = non-gonococcal urethritis. It is a rapid presumptive test only — always confirm with NAAT/culture.
SEXUAL HEALTH / GUM__Syphilis Serology (:
Syphilis serology combines two classes of blood test to diagnose, stage and monitor infection with Treponema pallidum. TREPONEMAL tests (EIA/CLIA screen, TPPA confirm) detect antibody specific to the organism and usually stay positive for life; NON-TREPONEMAL tests (RPR/VDRL) detect cardiolipin antibody, are quantitative (reported as a titre) and reflect current disease ACTIVITY, so they fall with successful treatment. Interpreting the two together, alongside the clinical history, allows diagnosis, staging and monitoring of treatment response.

1Indication & principle

Used to diagnose and stage syphilis (primary, secondary, latent, tertiary), screen at-risk and pregnant patients, and monitor response to therapy. Two complementary antibody targets are exploited:

🧪Treponemal (EIA/CLIA, TPPA)
Antibody specific to T. pallidum; confirms exposure; stays positive for life
📉Non-treponemal (RPR/VDRL)
Anti-cardiolipin antibody; quantitative titre; tracks disease activity & treatment
2How it is performed
A serum sample is first tested with an automated treponemal immunoassay (EIA/CLIA) as the screen.
A reactive screen is confirmed with a second treponemal test (TPPA) to exclude assay false positives.
A non-treponemal test (RPR or VDRL) is then performed and, if reactive, titrated by serial doubling dilutions (e.g. 1:2, 1:4, 1:8 ... 1:64) to give a baseline quantitative titre.
The baseline RPR titre is used as the reference for monitoring; repeat RPR after treatment should ideally use the same laboratory method.
3Interpretation
Treponemal positive + RPR positive (high titre)→Active / recent syphilis — treat
Treponemal positive + RPR negative→Treated / late latent, or very early infection — interpret with history
≥4-fold (2-dilution) FALL in RPR titre after treatment→Successful treatment response
≥4-fold RISE in RPR titre→Reinfection or treatment failure
Treponemal positive, no titre change, remains reactive for life→Cannot distinguish old treated from new infection — use RPR titre + history

First-line treatment of active syphilis is intramuscular benzathine penicillin.

4Pitfalls, limitations & safety
Because treponemal tests stay positive lifelong, a positive result never by itself confirms active disease — the quantitative RPR/VDRL titre and clinical history determine activity.
Neurosyphilis requires CSF examination (including CSF-VDRL) and congenital syphilis requires specific neonatal assessment; peripheral serology alone does not exclude them.
🚩 Non-treponemal (RPR/VDRL) tests give BIOLOGICAL FALSE POSITIVES in pregnancy, autoimmune disease (e.g. antiphospholipid syndrome / SLE) and other infections. The PROZONE phenomenon — antibody excess in very high-titre (often secondary) syphilis — can cause a FALSE-NEGATIVE RPR unless the serum is diluted. Always confirm with a treponemal test and request dilution when clinical suspicion is high.
🎓 Treponemal tests (EIA/TPPA) confirm exposure and stay positive for life; non-treponemal RPR/VDRL titres track activity and treatment — a 4-fold FALL = cure, a 4-fold RISE = reinfection/failure. Beware biological false positives and the prozone effect.
SEXUAL HEALTH / GUM__Dark-field Microsco:
Dark-field microscopy and PCR are direct detection tests for Treponema pallidum, the spirochaete of syphilis. They identify the organism itself in fluid taken straight from an early lesion — a primary chancre or a moist secondary lesion — and are especially valuable because serology can be negative in very early primary syphilis, before the host has mounted a detectable antibody response.

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Used to confirm syphilis by direct detection when a suspicious ulcer or moist lesion is present, particularly early on when serology may not yet be positive. T. pallidum cannot be grown on routine culture, so diagnosis rests on visualising or amplifying the organism directly.

Dark-field microscopy: oblique lighting makes the thin, unstainable, live motile corkscrew spirochaete glow bright against a black background as it moves in serous lesion fluid.
PCR: amplifies T. pallidum DNA. It is more practical and more specific, and it is the test of choice for oral and rectal lesions, where harmless commensal treponemes would confound microscopy.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

Clean the lesion with saline (no antiseptic), then gently abrade or squeeze the base to express clear serous exudate — not blood or pus.

For dark-field: transfer fluid immediately to a slide and examine promptly on the fresh specimen by an experienced operator, because the spirochaetes must still be motile.
For PCR: collect exudate on a swab into the appropriate transport medium; it does not depend on live organisms, so it tolerates transport and delay far better.
Always take serology in parallel (e.g. treponemal EIA/TPPA plus RPR/VDRL) regardless of the direct test result.
3INTERPRETATION
Motile spiral organisms seen on dark-field of a genital chancre→Primary syphilis confirmed, even if serology is still negative
Oral or rectal lesion→Use PCR, not dark-field — commensal treponemes give false positives on microscopy
PainLESS indurated genital ulcer→Primary syphilitic chancre — sample it directly
Negative direct test→Does NOT exclude syphilis — repeat sampling and send/repeat serology
🔬Dark-field
Live motile spirochaete on fresh genital lesion fluid
🧬PCR
Detects T. pallidum DNA; best for oral/rectal sites
🩸Serology
Sent in parallel; may be negative in very early disease
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & SAFETY
Dark-field is operator-dependent and only reliable on fresh, promptly examined genital exudate.
Prior antiseptic or systemic antibiotics can render both tests falsely negative.
A dry, healing, or crusted ulcer yields too little serous fluid for a valid dark-field result.
🚩 Dark-field microscopy must be performed promptly on fresh lesion exudate by an experienced operator, and is UNRELIABLE on oral or rectal lesions because commensal spirochaetes cause false positives — use PCR there. A negative direct test does NOT exclude syphilis, so always send serology and repeat sampling. The lesion fluid is highly infectious — handle it with strict care and appropriate protection.
🎓 Dark-field and PCR detect T. pallidum directly from a chancre when serology may still be negative in early primary syphilis. Use PCR (not dark-field) for oral or rectal lesions. A painless indurated ulcer is a chancre until proven otherwise — sample it.
SEXUAL HEALTH / GUM__HSV PCR (Genital Le:
HSV PCR is a molecular test performed on a swab taken from a genital lesion to confirm herpes simplex virus infection and to determine the viral type. It answers two clinical questions at once: is this ulcer/vesicle caused by HSV, and is it HSV-1 or HSV-2? Typing matters because it guides prognosis and counselling — HSV-2 recurs more frequently than HSV-1.

1Indication & principle

Used to confirm and type genital herpes in a patient presenting with painful genital vesicles or ulcers, especially a painful first (primary) episode. PCR amplifies and detects HSV DNA directly from the lesion, and modern type-specific assays distinguish HSV-1 from HSV-2. PCR has largely replaced viral culture because it is far more sensitive and gives a rapid, reliable result even from small amounts of virus.

Confirms the diagnosis when the clinical picture is uncertain (herpes vs other causes of genital ulceration).
Types the virus: HSV-1 vs HSV-2 — informs recurrence risk and counselling.
Far more sensitive than culture, which it has now largely replaced.
2How it is performed

An active lesion is chosen. A vesicle should be de-roofed and the swab firmly rolled over the base of the vesicle or ulcer to collect infected epithelial cells, then placed in viral transport medium and sent for PCR. Sampling technique is critical — the base of a fresh lesion carries the highest viral load, so early swabbing of a moist lesion gives the best yield.

🧪Lesion base swab
De-roof a vesicle and swab the base for maximum viral yield.
🧬PCR detection
Amplifies HSV DNA — sensitive even at low viral load.
🔬Type-specific
Distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2 to guide prognosis.
3Interpretation
Painful grouped vesicles/ulcers on an erythematous base, especially a painful FIRST episode with systemic upset→Genital herpes — swab the lesion base for HSV PCR
HSV-2 detected→More frequent recurrences — discuss suppressive antiviral therapy
Primary (first) episode confirmed→Start oral aciclovir (or valaciclovir) early
Swab taken from a dry / crusted / healing lesion→Reduced viral shedding — lower yield, a negative result does not exclude HSV
4Pitfalls & safety
Sampling error is the commonest cause of a false-negative — always swab the base, not the surface crust.
A crusted or healing lesion sheds little virus, so a negative PCR cannot rule out herpes.
Painful ulceration favours HSV; a painless indurated ulcer (chancre) should prompt testing for syphilis.
🚩 Genital herpes in late pregnancy risks NEONATAL HERPES. A primary episode in the third trimester warrants aciclovir and consideration of CAESAREAN delivery to reduce vertical transmission. A negative PCR from a crusted or healing lesion does NOT exclude HSV. Remember: painful ulcers point to herpes, whereas the painless ulcer of syphilis is a key discriminator.
🎓 HSV PCR from the lesion base both confirms and TYPES genital herpes (HSV-1 vs HSV-2). Painful grouped vesicles/ulcers = herpes (vs the painless chancre = syphilis). Treat with aciclovir; a third-trimester primary episode risks neonatal herpes and may need caesarean delivery.
SEXUAL HEALTH / GUM__Scabies — Dermoscop:
Scabies is an intensely itchy contagious skin infestation caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei var. hominis, which burrows into the epidermis. Dermoscopy and skin scraping are simple bedside confirmatory tests: dermoscopy visualises the mite at the end of a burrow as the classic delta-wing (jet-with-contrail) sign, while a scraping of a burrow examined in potassium hydroxide (KOH) under the microscope reveals mites, eggs or faecal pellets (scybala).

1INDICATION & PRINCIPLE

Suspect scabies in a patient with widespread intensely itchy papules and linear burrows, classically with itch worse at night and a history of other household or close contacts also itching. The pruritus is a delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, its eggs and faeces, so it may appear 3–6 weeks after first infestation.

The female mite tunnels through the stratum corneum, leaving a short grey-white serpiginous burrow with the mite at its leading end.
Confirmation matters because treatment involves the patient plus all contacts, and mimics (eczema, papular urticaria) are treated differently.
2HOW IT IS PERFORMED

First identify a burrow at typical sites – finger webs, flexor wrists, genitalia, axillae, areolae and periumbilical skin. A dermoscope is placed over the burrow at high magnification to look for the mite at its end. For a skin scraping, apply a drop of mineral oil or KOH to the burrow, scrape it firmly with a scalpel blade onto a glass slide, add a coverslip and examine under low-power microscopy.

Dermoscopy is non-invasive, rapid and increasingly the first-line confirmatory test.
Scraping is more definitive but operator-dependent; sampling several fresh burrows raises the yield.
3INTERPRETATION
Intensely itchy burrows in finger webs, wrists, genitalia, axillae→Classic clinical scabies
Dermoscopy: delta-wing / jet-with-contrail sign at the end of a burrow→Mite head visualised – confirms diagnosis
KOH scraping showing mite, eggs or faecal pellets on microscopy→Confirmatory (positive) result
Thick hyperkeratotic crusted plaques teeming with mites in an immunocompromised/elderly patient→Crusted (Norwegian) scabies – enormous mite burden, highly contagious
🔺Delta-wing sign
Dark triangular mite head at the burrow end resembling a jet with a contrail
🥚Eggs
Oval ova within the burrow seen on KOH microscopy
💩Scybala
Faecal pellets trailing behind the mite – a confirmatory finding
🧴Permethrin 5%
First-line topical treatment, applied to whole body and repeated after 1 week
4PITFALLS, LIMITATIONS & TREATMENT

A negative scraping does not exclude scabies – classical disease often carries only 5–15 mites, so sampling may miss them; diagnosis remains largely clinical. Excoriation, secondary eczematisation and impetiginisation can obscure burrows. Treat with topical permethrin 5% cream applied to the whole body from the neck down (including under nails) and washed off after 8–12 hours, then repeated after 1 week. Treat all close/household and sexual contacts simultaneously, and wash bedding and clothing at a hot temperature (≥50°C) or seal in a bag for 72 hours.

🚩 Crusted (Norwegian) scabies carries an enormous mite burden and is extremely contagious, causing institutional outbreaks – it needs patient isolation and combined topical permethrin plus oral ivermectin, with treatment of all contacts. Always treat ALL household and sexual contacts at the same time even if asymptomatic, and warn the patient that itch can persist for several weeks after successful eradication (post-scabetic itch) – this is not treatment failure.
🎓 The dermoscopy delta-wing (jet-with-contrail) sign and a KOH skin scraping showing mites, eggs or faeces confirm scabies. Think of it with burrows in finger webs, wrists and genitals plus nocturnal itch and affected contacts. Treat with permethrin (repeat at 1 week) and treat all contacts simultaneously; crusted scabies is hugely contagious and needs ivermectin plus permethrin.
SEXUAL HEALTH / GUM__Test of Cure & Part:
Test of cure (TOC) and partner notification are the two pillars of safe STI follow-up. A test of cure re-tests the treated patient in specific situations to confirm the organism has actually been eradicated, while partner notification (contact tracing) identifies, tests and treats sexual contacts to break onward transmission and prevent reinfection of the index patient. Together they turn a single consultation into effective infection control.

1Indication & principle

A microbiological cure cannot be assumed from symptom resolution alone. TOC is targeted at situations where treatment failure or resistance is likely, or where the stakes of persistence are high (pregnancy, congenital risk, rising antimicrobial resistance). Partner notification rests on the principle that an STI is shared within a sexual network: unless contacts are treated, the index patient is simply re-exposed.

TOC confirms eradication where resistance or failure is plausible.
Partner notification breaks the transmission chain and prevents reinfection.
Both are core, confidential elements of GUM/sexual-health care.
2Who needs a test of cure
Gonorrhoea (all cases)→TOC recommended for everyone (culture ± NAAT) given rising antimicrobial resistance
Mycoplasma genitalium→TOC indicated (macrolide resistance common) — NAAT ~3-5 weeks post-treatment
Syphilis→Follow with serial RPR/VDRL titres; a fourfold (2 dilution) fall confirms response
Chlamydia in pregnancy→TOC indicated to protect the pregnancy and neonate
Uncomplicated chlamydia (non-pregnant)→Routine TOC NOT needed — instead re-test at ~3 months for reinfection
3Timing & interpretation of TOC

The commonest TOC error is testing too early with a NAAT. NAATs detect nucleic acid whether or not the organism is alive, so residual dead DNA/RNA from successfully killed organisms can give a false-positive result if sampled prematurely.

NAAT-based TOC < 2 weeks post-treatment→Unreliable — risk of false positive from non-viable residual nucleic acid
NAAT-based TOC at ~2-5 weeks→Recommended window — residual nucleic acid has cleared, result is meaningful
Gonorrhoea culture positive on TOC→Confirms treatment failure/resistance — allows sensitivities and guided re-treatment
4Partner notification in practice

Trace, test and treat sexual contacts within the relevant look-back period, offering current partners epidemiological (empirical) treatment without waiting for their results. It may be provider-referral (clinic contacts the partner) or patient-referral (index patient informs them), always maintaining confidentiality.

🧪Chlamydia
Look-back ~6 months (or last partner); treat contacts empirically
🧫Gonorrhoea
Look-back ~2 weeks (symptomatic) to 3 months; test and treat contacts
🩸Syphilis
Look-back tailored to stage (up to 2 years in late latent)
🚫Abstinence
No sex until patient and partner(s) treated and follow-up complete
🚩 Do NOT perform a NAAT test of cure too early: residual non-viable nucleic acid persists after successful treatment and gives a FALSE-POSITIVE result — wait the recommended interval (about 2-5 weeks). Failure to notify and treat partners leads to reinfection and ongoing transmission, so partner notification is a core, confidential part of STI management. Advise the patient and partners to abstain from sex until all are treated.
🎓 TOC is needed for gonorrhoea, Mycoplasma genitalium, syphilis (serial RPR titres) and chlamydia in pregnancy — but NOT for routine uncomplicated chlamydia (re-test at ~3 months instead). Wait 2-5 weeks before a NAAT TOC to avoid false positives from dead DNA, and complete partner notification within the look-back period to break transmission and prevent reinfection.
